basic_information.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
basic_information.creator: OpenAI (successor to experimental Swarm framework, maintained by OpenAI core team)
basic_information.release_date: March 11, 2025 (initial release on GitHub; announced alongside Responses API and new tools for building agents)

technical_architecture.architecture_pattern: multi_agent | orchestrator | code_first — The SDK uses a minimalist, code-first approach with very few abstractions built around three primitives: Agents (LLMs with instructions and tools), Handoffs (delegation between agents), and Guardrails (input/output validation). Supports two multi-agent patterns: Manager mode (central orchestrator invokes sub-agents as tools, retains control) and Handoff mode (peer agents transfer control to specialists in a decentralized fashion). Designed for deterministic flows, iterative loops, and flexible LLM workflows.
technical_architecture.underlying_models: Provider-agnostic. Natively supports OpenAI models via Responses API and Chat Completions API (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, o-series reasoning models). Supports 100+ LLMs via official LiteLLM extension (pip install openai-agents[litellm]) including: Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Mistral, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Cohere, Groq, Together AI, and local models. Also supports any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint via set_default_openai_client() or custom ModelProvider at the Runner.run level. Requires openai v2.x (v1.x no longer supported as of v0.7.0).
technical_architecture.tool_integration: Native function-calling tool system. MCP (Model Context Protocol) support built-in with three transport options: stdio (local servers), Streamable HTTP (remote servers), and HostedMCPTool (OpenAI-hosted MCP with connectors). Supports aggregating tools from multiple MCP servers. OpenAI hosted tools include web search, file search, code interpreter, and computer use. Custom tools defined as Python functions with type annotations. Tool guardrails can wrap any tool for pre/post-execution validation.
technical_architecture.planning_approach: ReAct — Agents follow a Reasoning + Acting loop with tool calls. The SDK itself is not opinionated about planning methodology; it provides the execution infrastructure and lets the underlying LLM handle planning. Supports iterative agent loops, deterministic flows, and multi-step tool use. No built-in tree-of-thought or graph-based planning; relies on the LLM's native reasoning capabilities (enhanced when using o-series reasoning models). The lightweight design intentionally avoids imposing planning abstractions.
technical_architecture.multi_agent_support: First-class multi-agent support via two patterns: (1) Handoffs — agents transfer full conversation control to specialist agents (decentralized, peer-to-peer). Handoffs are defined on each agent and can include input filters for context management. (2) Agents-as-tools — a manager agent invokes sub-agents as tools, retains control of the conversation, and synthesizes results (centralized orchestrator). Agents can be nested and composed. No built-in parallel agent execution; parallelism is handled at the tool/guardrail level (guardrails run concurrently with agent execution).

memory_and_context.memory_types_supported: short_term (conversation via Sessions) | semantic (via external vector stores) — Built-in session memory automatically maintains conversation history across multiple agent runs without manual state management. Sessions store dialog history, tool call results, and agent outputs. Long-term memory is not built-in but supported via external integrations: Mem0 for episodic memory, Pinecone/vector databases for semantic memory. RunContextWrapper allows structured state objects to persist across runs for procedural context.
memory_and_context.context_window_management: Two built-in techniques: (1) Trimming — removes older messages to stay within context limits. (2) Compression/Summarization — compresses past conversation into summaries, retaining long-range memory compactly (past requirements, decisions, rationales persist beyond N turns). Sessions handle context length automatically. Developers can configure these strategies per session. Context summarization is particularly useful for long-running agents where the agent needs to 'remember' commitments and constraints from early in the conversation.
memory_and_context.persistence_mechanism: database | in_memory — Default session implementation uses SQLite (either in-memory or persistent file-based). Production sessions available via SQLAlchemy-supported databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc.) with encryption and TTL (time-to-live) configuration. External persistence via Mem0, Pinecone, or custom vector stores for long-term memory across sessions. RunContextWrapper provides in-process state persistence across runs.
memory_and_context.context_engineering_approach: Context is treated as a first-class architectural concern via the Sessions system. OpenAI's official cookbook explicitly frames this as 'Context Engineering' — the session becomes the memory object, and the SDK handles context length, history, and continuity automatically. Two-layer approach: short-term context via Sessions (automatic), long-term context via external memory stores (configurable). Handoff history management is configurable (opt-in nested history vs. flat history via RunConfig). The SDK provides building blocks rather than prescribing a single context strategy.

capabilities.core_capabilities: Lightweight agent definition with instructions, tools, and model configuration. Handoffs for inter-agent delegation (both peer-to-peer and hierarchical). Three types of guardrails: input (user input validation), output (final output validation), and tool (pre/post tool execution validation). Built-in tracing for debugging, monitoring, and evaluation. Sessions for automatic conversation history management. Human-in-the-loop approval mechanism for sensitive tool executions. Realtime/Voice Agents with speech-to-speech models, automatic interruption detection, and context management. Structured output support via Pydantic models or JSON schema. Async and streaming execution support. Built-in OpenAI hosted tools: web search, file search (vector store), code interpreter, computer use. Provider-agnostic model support via LiteLLM. SIP protocol support for telephony voice agents (v0.7.0+). Python 3.14 compatibility.
capabilities.supported_modalities: Text, code (via code interpreter), vision (via multimodal models), voice/speech (via Realtime Agents with speech-to-speech), web browsing (via computer use tool), file system (via file search and code interpreter). Voice agents support automatic interruption detection and SIP telephony connections.
capabilities.autonomy_level: human_in_loop | supervised | fully_autonomous — Configurable per tool and per agent run. Tools can set needsApproval=true to require human approval before execution. The SDK supports pausing execution, serializing agent state, obtaining approval/rejection, and resuming. Guardrails provide automated supervision. Default mode is fully autonomous within defined tool/instruction scope.
capabilities.tool_ecosystem: OpenAI hosted tools: web search, file search (with vector stores), code interpreter, computer use. MCP server ecosystem provides access to thousands of community tools. LiteLLM integration for 100+ LLM providers. Third-party tool libraries via Composio, ArcadeAI, and others. Custom tools are simple Python functions with type annotations. Tool guardrails add validation layers. HostedMCPTool connects to remote MCP servers with authentication via OpenAI connectors.

agent_interoperability.mcp_support: Yes — first-class MCP support. Three transport modes: stdio (local MCP servers), Streamable HTTP (remote servers), and HostedMCPTool (OpenAI-managed MCP with connectors and authentication). Can aggregate tools from multiple MCP servers simultaneously. OpenAI adopted MCP across Agents SDK, Responses API, and ChatGPT desktop in March 2025. Local MCP tool failure handling is configurable (v0.7.0+): can return model-visible error output instead of failing the entire run.
agent_interoperability.a2a_support: No native A2A protocol support as of v0.8.1. The OpenAI Agents SDK does not implement Google's Agent2Agent protocol. OpenAI has not publicly announced plans to adopt A2A. Multi-agent communication is handled via the SDK's own handoff and agents-as-tools mechanisms rather than an inter-framework protocol. [uncertain]
agent_interoperability.agents_md_support: Yes — via OpenAI Codex integration. Codex reads AGENTS.md files (and AGENTS.override.md) before executing tasks, walking from project root to working directory. AGENTS.md serves as project-specific instructions for coding agents. The Agents SDK itself does not natively parse AGENTS.md, but the Codex product built on the Agents SDK does. The agents.md specification (agents.md open format) is supported in the OpenAI ecosystem.
agent_interoperability.cross_framework_compatibility: Moderate. MCP support enables tool sharing with any MCP-compatible framework (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, etc.). LiteLLM integration provides universal LLM provider compatibility. No A2A protocol support limits direct agent-to-agent communication with frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, or Google ADK that implement A2A. The SDK is designed as a standalone orchestration layer rather than a protocol-interoperable node. Can be embedded in larger systems or used alongside other frameworks at the infrastructure level.

safety_and_guardrails.permission_model: capability_based | sandbox — Agents are granted specific tools at creation time. Tool access is explicitly defined per agent. Tool guardrails can block or modify tool calls before execution. HostedMCPTool supports approval requirements for external tool access. Code interpreter runs in a sandboxed environment. No universal allow/deny list system; permissions are scoped per agent and per tool.
safety_and_guardrails.escalation_policy: Configurable via human-in-the-loop approval mechanism. Tools marked with needsApproval trigger execution pause and human review. Agent state can be serialized, stored, and resumed after human decision. Guardrails use 'tripwire' pattern — when a check fails, execution halts immediately (fail-fast). No built-in SLA or tiered escalation system; escalation logic is left to application code.
safety_and_guardrails.hallucination_mitigation: Multi-layered approach: (1) Output guardrails validate final agent output against quality/accuracy criteria. (2) Tool guardrails verify tool call results before they re-enter the agent loop. (3) Structured output enforcement via Pydantic models constrains response format. (4) OpenAI Guardrails package provides built-in hallucination detection using vector stores. (5) Prompt engineering best practices documented in official safety guide: strengthen prompts with clear policies, examples, and edge case handling. (6) File search tool with citations reduces hallucination by grounding responses in source documents.
safety_and_guardrails.audit_trail: Yes — built-in tracing captures comprehensive records of all agent events: LLM generations, tool calls, handoffs, guardrail triggers, and custom events. Traces are viewable in the OpenAI Traces dashboard. Exportable to external systems via trace processors. Configurable sensitive data handling (trace_include_sensitive_data flag). Batch processing via BatchTraceProcessor.
safety_and_guardrails.human_oversight_pattern: pre-approval | post-review | always_on — (1) Pre-approval: tools with needsApproval require human sign-off before execution. (2) Post-review: output guardrails validate results after generation. (3) Tool guardrails provide both pre-execution (input) and post-execution (output) review. (4) Agent state serialization allows offline human review and resume. (5) Tracing provides post-hoc audit capability. The SDK provides the primitives; the specific oversight pattern is chosen by the developer.

governance_and_standards.governance_body: OpenAI (private company). No external standards body governance. The SDK is open-source under MIT license but development is led by OpenAI's internal team. MCP protocol governed by Anthropic. No formal affiliation with AAIF, Linux Foundation, or ISO for the SDK itself.
governance_and_standards.contributing_protocols: Implements MCP (Model Context Protocol) by Anthropic for tool interoperability. Supports OpenAI Responses API and Chat Completions API. Tracing system is compatible with external observability standards. Does not implement A2A, OpenTelemetry natively, or other formal inter-agent protocols.
governance_and_standards.regulatory_compliance: Inherits OpenAI platform compliance: SOC 2 Type II (for API Platform, ChatGPT Enterprise/Team/Edu), GDPR alignment via Data Processing Addendum, CSA STAR certification. OpenAI has published EU AI Act compliance guidance and prohibited practices documentation. The SDK itself is a client-side library with no independent compliance certifications — compliance depends on the deployment context and OpenAI API usage. Sensitive data handling in traces is configurable (OPENAI_AGENTS_DISABLE_TRACING or trace_include_sensitive_data=False for PII/PHI workflows). [uncertain]

deployment_and_operations.deployment_modes: local | cloud | hybrid — The SDK is a Python library that runs anywhere Python runs (local machines, cloud VMs, containers, serverless functions). LLM inference is via API calls to OpenAI or other providers. No managed deployment service specific to the Agents SDK (unlike CrewAI AMP). Can be deployed with any Python hosting solution. Docker-compatible. Integrates with Temporal for durable execution in production.
deployment_and_operations.scalability_model: horizontal | serverless — Standard Python scaling patterns apply (asyncio, multiprocessing, container orchestration). Async execution support for concurrent agent runs. No built-in distributed orchestration; relies on external infrastructure (Kubernetes, serverless platforms, Temporal). Session persistence via SQLAlchemy supports connection pooling for high-throughput scenarios.
deployment_and_operations.cost_per_task: SDK itself is free (MIT license). Costs are entirely LLM API usage: OpenAI GPT-4o-mini at $0.15/$0.60 per 1M tokens (input/output), GPT-4o at $2.50/$10 per 1M tokens, o-series reasoning models at higher rates. Code interpreter, web search, and file search have additional per-use charges (e.g., code interpreter at ~$0.03/session, file search at $0.025/GB/day for vector storage). Computer use tool at $3/$12 per 1M tokens. A simple single-agent task with GPT-4o-mini costs fractions of a cent; complex multi-agent workflows with GPT-4o can cost $0.10-$2.00+ per execution.
deployment_and_operations.resource_requirements: Lightweight — Python 3.9+ required (3.14 compatible as of v0.7.0). No GPU required (all LLM inference is via API). Minimal RAM requirements (the SDK itself is a thin orchestration layer). Dependencies: openai v2.x, pydantic, httpx. Optional: SQLAlchemy for production sessions, litellm for multi-provider support. Network connectivity required for API calls.

observability_and_ops.monitoring_integration: Built-in tracing sends to OpenAI Traces dashboard by default. Extensive third-party integration via trace processors: Langfuse (open-source, batch trace processor), Braintrust (trace processors for comprehensive monitoring), AgentOps (production agent monitoring with session replays), LangSmith (LangChain ecosystem), W&B Weave (Weights & Biases), Logfire (Pydantic ecosystem), Scorecard, Keywords AI, and more. Custom trace processors can be implemented for any destination.
observability_and_ops.tracing_support: Yes — built-in, on by default. Traces capture: LLM generations (with token counts), tool calls and results, handoffs between agents, guardrail executions, custom spans. Viewable in OpenAI Traces dashboard. Exportable via BatchTraceProcessor to external systems. Configurable sensitive data handling. Extensible with custom spans. Supports evaluation, fine-tuning, and distillation workflows based on trace data.
observability_and_ops.production_readiness_level: production_ready — Explicitly positioned as the production-ready evolution of Swarm. Active development with frequent releases (5+ releases in January-February 2026 alone). Used by enterprise customers including Box for document intelligence agents. Backed by OpenAI with long-term commitment. However, still at v0.x (pre-1.0), indicating API may still have breaking changes (e.g., nested handoff history default changed in v0.7.0, openai v1.x support dropped). Python and TypeScript SDKs both available.

adoption_and_market.adoption_scale: 18,848 GitHub stars, 3,146 forks, 210 contributors (GitHub API-verified). Available on PyPI as openai-agents. TypeScript SDK also available as @openai/agents on npm. Swarm (predecessor) was 'widely adopted by the developer community and successfully deployed by multiple customers' before being superseded. Specific PyPI download numbers not publicly available but significant given OpenAI's developer ecosystem reach. Box, financial services firms, and other enterprise customers using the SDK in production.
adoption_and_market.pricing_model: open-source (MIT) — The SDK itself is completely free. Users pay only for LLM API usage (OpenAI API pricing or other provider costs). No SDK-specific licensing fees, no tiered SDK plans. Enterprise features (SSO, RBAC, audit logs) are included at no additional fee in the OpenAI API platform. OpenAI API has usage-based pricing with different tiers for different models.
adoption_and_market.key_use_cases: Customer service automation (triage agent routing to specialists — official demo available on GitHub). Voice/phone support agents with Realtime Agents and SIP telephony. Document intelligence and enterprise search (Box integration). Financial analysis with multi-source data aggregation. Coding agents (Codex built on Agents SDK). Multi-step research and analysis workflows. Content generation pipelines. Browser-based automation via computer use tool. Internal knowledge assistants with file search and RAG.
adoption_and_market.competitive_position: Positioned as the simplest and most lightweight major agent framework. Strengths: minimal abstractions (fastest to learn), official OpenAI backing (best integration with OpenAI models and tools), built-in tracing and evaluation pipeline, voice/realtime agent support. Weaknesses: less sophisticated state management than LangGraph, no built-in parallel agent execution, pre-1.0 with potential breaking changes, weaker multi-provider support than LangChain ecosystem. Competitive with LangGraph (more complex but more powerful), CrewAI (similar ease of use but different paradigm), AutoGen (conversation-focused), and AWS Strands Agents. Nearly matched LangGraph in efficiency benchmarks while being easier to use.

ecosystem_maturity.community_size: 18,848 GitHub stars, 210 contributors, 3,146 forks (Python SDK). TypeScript SDK also active. OpenAI Developer Forum for Q&A and discussion. OpenAI Discord server with Developers' Corner channels. OpenAI Cookbook with Agents SDK examples and tutorials. Growing rapidly since March 2025 launch (~11 months). Backed by OpenAI's massive developer community (millions of API users).
ecosystem_maturity.documentation_quality: excellent — Comprehensive official documentation at openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ covering all concepts: agents, handoffs, guardrails, sessions, tracing, MCP, voice agents, models. OpenAI Cookbook provides practical examples (session memory, context engineering, customer service demo, voice assistant). OpenAI platform docs (platform.openai.com) include Agents SDK guides. API reference auto-generated. Safety guide for production deployment. Multiple cookbooks for advanced patterns.
ecosystem_maturity.third_party_integrations_count: 10+ official tracing integrations (Langfuse, Braintrust, AgentOps, LangSmith, W&B Weave, Logfire, Scorecard, Keywords AI, etc.). MCP ecosystem provides access to thousands of community-built tool servers. 100+ LLM providers via LiteLLM. OpenAI hosted tools (web search, file search, code interpreter, computer use). Composio and ArcadeAI for additional tool integrations. Temporal integration for durable execution. Mem0 for long-term memory.
ecosystem_maturity.tutorial_availability: excellent — Official OpenAI Cookbook with hands-on examples (voice assistant, customer service, session memory, context personalization). Platform documentation with quickstart guide. Data Science Dojo, DigitalOcean, Medium, Towards Data Science, and Dev.to tutorials widely available. YouTube walkthroughs. Composio, Langfuse, and Braintrust publish integration-specific tutorials. Official examples directory in GitHub repo covers: basic agents, multi-agent handoffs, guardrails, streaming, MCP integration.

human_agent_interaction.autonomy_spectrum: assistant (executes with approval) | autonomous (acts independently) — Default: autonomous within defined tool and instruction scope. With needsApproval on tools: assistant mode requiring human sign-off. Guardrails provide automated oversight. The spectrum is configurable per tool, per agent, making it flexible from fully autonomous to heavily supervised.
human_agent_interaction.handoff_mechanism: Two mechanisms: (1) Agent-to-agent handoffs: agents transfer conversation control to specialist agents via defined handoff targets. Handoffs can filter input context and customize behavior per target. (2) Agent-to-human: tools with needsApproval pause execution and serialize state. Human reviews the pending tool call, approves or rejects, and execution resumes. State is fully serializable for async human review (can persist to database, review later, resume). Guardrail tripwires also halt execution for human intervention.
human_agent_interaction.feedback_loop: Session memory accumulates conversation history across runs, enabling agents to learn from interaction patterns within a session. Long-term improvement via: tracing data used for evaluation and fine-tuning (trace-to-distillation pipeline), prompt iteration based on trace analysis, structured output validation catching error patterns. No built-in RLHF or automated feedback-to-model-improvement. Improvement is developer-driven through trace analysis, prompt refinement, and guardrail tuning.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: Very high applicability for startups building AI-powered products. USE WHEN: (1) You want the fastest path from zero to working agent (minimal boilerplate, few abstractions), (2) Your primary LLM is OpenAI and you want best-in-class integration (tracing, evaluation, fine-tuning pipeline), (3) You need voice/phone agents (Realtime Agents with SIP support are unique in the framework space), (4) You need customer service automation with multi-agent routing, (5) Your team values simplicity over maximum configurability, (6) You want MCP tool interoperability out of the box. AVOID WHEN: (1) You need complex state management and graph-based workflows (use LangGraph), (2) You are committed to non-OpenAI models as primary provider (SDK works but is optimized for OpenAI), (3) You need conversation-driven multi-agent debate/research (use AutoGen), (4) You need role-based agent teams with built-in delegation (use CrewAI), (5) You need enterprise managed deployment (no CrewAI AMP equivalent). STARTUP ADVANTAGE: MIT license, zero framework cost, OpenAI's ecosystem (largest LLM developer community), production tracing built-in from day one, voice agent capability is a differentiator for telephony startups.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy: BUILD with OpenAI Agents SDK when: you have Python/TypeScript developers, want minimal framework overhead, are already using OpenAI APIs, and need voice agents or MCP integration. The SDK is 'build' — it provides primitives, not pre-built solutions. ALTERNATIVE frameworks: LangGraph for maximum control and complex state, CrewAI for role-based teams and managed deployment, AutoGen for research/conversation agents, Strands Agents (AWS) for AWS-native deployments. COST: SDK is free; total cost = OpenAI API usage. A simple customer service agent with GPT-4o-mini can run for <$5/day in API costs at moderate volume. Compare to CrewAI AMP at $99-$10K+/month or building custom orchestration from scratch (weeks of engineering time).
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 4 (AI business models & strategy) — Illustrates OpenAI's developer platform strategy and open-source-as-ecosystem-growth model. Session 3 (AI project framing) — key framework for Build vs Buy decisions in agent development, CRISP-DM implementation. Session 5 (ethics and governance) — guardrails, safety patterns, and human oversight in agentic systems.

confidence.data_quality: High — based on official OpenAI documentation (openai.github.io/openai-agents-python, platform.openai.com, cookbook.openai.com), GitHub API-verified repository statistics, PyPI package metadata, official OpenAI blog posts and announcements, and reputable tech publications (InfoQ, VentureBeat, Towards Data Science, DigitalOcean).
confidence.cross_reference: GitHub API confirms 18,848 stars, MIT license, 210 contributors, 3,146 forks (queried February 9, 2026). Version 0.8.1 confirmed via GitHub releases (February 6, 2026). March 11, 2025 release date confirmed by multiple sources (InfoQ, Analytics Vidhya, official OpenAI blog). MCP support confirmed by official documentation and OpenAI Developers X/Twitter announcement. LiteLLM integration confirmed by official docs and LiteLLM documentation. Competitive benchmarking data from Composio, Langfuse, and multiple independent comparison articles.
confidence.caveats: Pre-1.0 version (v0.8.1) means API breaking changes are still possible — e.g., v0.7.0 dropped openai v1.x support, changed nested handoff history defaults, and changed reasoning.effort defaults. GitHub stars (18.8K) are lower than competitors like CrewAI (43.8K) and LangGraph, partly because it launched 18 months after CrewAI. Specific PyPI download statistics were not available for independent verification. A2A protocol support status could not be definitively confirmed — absence of documentation suggests no support, but OpenAI may add it in the future. The framework is evolving rapidly with frequent releases.
